record.file_problem: The supplied text is cut off at the end; the relevant main-text and supplementary scaling-law sections are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study fits and evaluates scaling laws on its own molecular masked-language-model training runs, and reports that the fitted model/data balance differs from published NLP results and changes with fitting formulation. This is a refinement of the scope of the claimed laws.
record.gate_note: The study measures validation cross-entropy scaling and compute-optimal allocation for MIST. It also reports downstream and chemical-property results, but those do not test downstream predictability from pretraining loss or model scale. Hyperparameter values used to choose training configurations are not recorded as separate outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study fits Hoffmann-style loss laws to 138 of its own SMILES masked-language-model pretraining runs (393k–603M parameters, 8M–2B molecules). It derives compute-optimal allocations and compares several fitting formulations. This makes it a new setting (molecular SMILES) with its own results on V3, V5 and V7. It also argues, with a Zipf/peeling-decoding theorem, that low data quality shifts the compute-optimal split toward data, which is a T5-type restatement of V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that hyperparameter-penalized Bayesian scaling laws fit better than unpenalized ones and cut scaling-law compute by about 10×. For MIST, α/β ≈ 1.75 implies data should scale faster than model size, departing from NLP's ≈1. They read α ≈ 1 as variance-limited model scaling and β ≈ 0.54 as resolution-limited data scaling on a low-dimensional manifold, and conclude that limited corpus quality and diversity is the bottleneck. They support this with a Zipf concept-frequency theorem predicting D ∝ N^θ for θ > 1.
record.recipe_differences: Adapts the Hoffmann-style loss law to molecular masked-language-model pretraining, counts D as molecules rather than tokens, adds quadratic penalties for hyperparameter deviations, and fits parameters with Bayesian MCMC rather than only point-estimate nonlinear fitting.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with penalty inclusion and formulation, and with whether the learning-rate scaling uses parameter count or hidden size. Dataset size D is counted as molecules; the authors note it could be rescaled by the average 65.2 ± 9.57 tokens per molecule.

fits_no_version.finding: The fitted optimal learning rate scales with batch size as δ = 0.55 [0.46, 0.63] and is nearly independent of N (γ = 0.04). When parameterized by hidden size, γ = -0.74 [-0.91, -0.56].
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal learning rate follows a power law in batch size (about square-root) and in model width.

record.problems: Evidence is from one molecular pretraining corpus and model family, not a general language-model replication. The fitting data count is molecules rather than tokens. Predictive accuracy is reported in aggregate and the supplied text does not provide a separately quantified held-out loss prediction for a named larger run. The authors also note that the pretraining dataset’s quality and coverage limit scaling efficiency.
record.rows_left_out: No additional scaling-law results relevant to the claim were left out; other reported MIST benchmark and application outcomes do not test these claim versions.

untested.parts: Natural-language text pretraining. The corpus is molecular SMILES, so no V1 claim about text language models is tested.
Prediction of much larger runs. MIST-228M was trained 'to validate' the laws and MIST-1.8B was sized from them, but no prediction error for either is reported.
Shape penalties (feed-forward ratio, aspect ratio, KQV size) are fitted and shown in Fig. 5c, but no numeric effect sizes appear in the text.
Image/video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer regimes.
Not tested by design; only incidental comparisons across two or three model sizes exist, with model and data size confounded.

missing.what: Other formulations: additive penalties (α/β 1.35 [0.951, 1.82], β 0.679, MAPE 38.1%, WAIC -464) and harmonic shape penalties (α/β 1.74, MAPE 28.2%). Across fits E ranges from 1.57e-3 to 29.9e-3.
Fits to smoothed (averaged) validation loss degrade WAIC and MAPE as the averaging window grows.
Use of the fitted law to size MIST-228M (a validation run) and MIST-1.8B, with the largest models starred in Fig. 5d/e. No quantified prediction error for these runs is given.
Fitted shape penalties Pff, Paspect and Pkv with 95% credible intervals (impact of shape on loss).

Downstream results by model size are mixed. Larger models gain on QM9 (Avg MAE 3.78 for 28M vs 1.77 for 1.8B, unfrozen) and partial charges (MAE 0.036, 0.031, 0.030 for 28M/228M/1.8B), but not on BACE or ESOL. Model and data size are confounded.

record.verdict_notes: Main correction: r5 reported β (0.537) as the compute exponent a; the true value is a = 0.366. r3/r4 are in-sample fit metrics, so V2 links were removed and V2 is listed as untested. The SMILES corpus places rows under V5 rather than V1. This is a single model family and corpus, and D is counted in molecules (about 65 tokens each). The NLP comparison values in Extended Data table 6 are cited and were not made rows.

versions.untested_parts: Tests loss scaling with model size and dataset size for MIST; does not establish token-count scaling independently of dataset size, or the claim across language models generally.

Reports aggregate fit/predictive-accuracy statistics and trains a larger MIST model after fitting; the provided text does not give a separately quantified held-out prediction error specifically for that larger run.
Tests the compute-optimal parameter/data allocation on MIST; does not establish the trend across language-model setups generally.
Tests scaling-law form in molecular SMILES masked-language-model pretraining only; does not test image/video, repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer regimes.
Tests fitting formulations and compares MIST’s fitted scaling balance with reported NLP values; does not test every parameter-counting, schedule, or data choice listed in the version.

rows.subject: MIST, Penalized Scaling eq. 6 (Baseline)

rows.operation_detail: Fit a hyperparameter-penalized Bayesian neural scaling law to validation-loss data.

conditions.value: 8M to 2B molecules in the fitting sweep

rows.measure: Fitted model-size and data-size loss exponents
rows.note: A fitted power-law loss form for MIST; the authors interpret α/β > 1 as data needing to scale faster than model size.
rows.check: V1 removed: the corpus is SMILES strings, not natural-language text, so it bears on V5 (other regimes), not V1. The power-law form is assumed and fitted, not tested against alternatives. D is counted in molecules, not tokens. Losses are minimum validation losses from runs with deliberately off-optimal hyperparameters, modelled by the penalty terms.

relationships.condition: MIST SMILES masked-LM pretraining, development runs 393k–603M parameters
relationships.reason: A two-term power law in N and D fits validation loss with posterior exponents α≈0.84–0.93 and β≈0.54–0.75 and Spearman 0.78–0.81 (r1, r2).
relationships.display_finding: Validation loss fitted a two-term power law with parameter exponents approximately 0.84–0.93, data exponents approximately 0.54–0.75 and Spearman correlations of 0.78–0.81.

relationships.condition: Fit accuracy of the power-law form in this molecular setting
relationships.reason: In-sample MAPE is 29.1% (penalized) to 38.5% (unpenalized) and E is poorly determined. A good fit needed hyperparameter penalty terms (r3, r4).
relationships.display_finding: In-sample MAPE was 29.1% with hyperparameter penalties versus 38.5% without them, while E remained poorly determined.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Fit accuracy of the power-law form in this molecular setting
source_check.reason: The MAPE values and uncertainty in E are reported, but do not establish a failure of the power-law form. Penalties improve fits across off-optimal hyperparameters; neither necessity of penalties for a good fit nor a departure from power-law scaling is demonstrated.

relationships.condition: Penalized baseline fit (the fit used to train MIST-1.8B)
relationships.reason: a = 0.366 and b = 0.634 with α/β = 1.75, interval excluding 1: data should grow faster than model size, unlike both Kaplan and Hoffmann. The authors attribute this to low data diversity (r5, r7).
relationships.display_finding: Parameter and token exponents were 0.366 and 0.634, with α/β=1.75 and an interval excluding 1, favoring faster data growth.

relationships.display_finding: Across fitting formulations, β spans 0.516–0.751, α/β spans 1.14–1.75, and E varies about 15-fold, yielding disagreement over equal allocation; exponents are also linked to data quality.
